edges.effect_quant: In 17 obese adults who did not routinely use non-nutritive sweeteners, sucralose taken before an oral glucose load increased peak glucose and insulin area under the curve and reduced insulin sensitivity by 23%; in a randomized trial of 66 healthy low-users, 14 days of sucralose reduced insulin sensitivity by a median 17.7% versus 2.8% in controls; and in a 10-week trial of 40 healthy adults, sucralose increased OGTT glucose area under the curve and serum insulin compared with water.
edges.population: adults without diabetes, especially low habitual users of non-nutritive sweeteners undergoing acute or short-term sucralose exposure before glucose testing
edges.mechanism: Sucralose may alter cephalic sweet signaling, incretin responses, microbiome composition, and insulin handling in a way that slightly worsens glycemic responses to a glucose challenge in susceptible settings.
edges.summary: Human sucralose trials do not all agree, but several controlled studies show modest worsening of insulin sensitivity or glucose handling after acute or short-term exposure. The overall signal is not large, yet it is consistent enough to justify a harmful lean rather than assuming complete metabolic neutrality.
edges.caveats: The strongest effects tend to appear in non-habitual users, obese participants, or longer-exposure designs, and many other studies have found no material change. This is a low-magnitude, context-dependent signal rather than a demonstration that ordinary sucralose use reliably causes dysglycemia in everyone.

evidence.citation: Pepino MY et al 2013 Diabetes Care
evidence.notes: Sucralose affects glycemic and hormonal responses to an oral glucose load.
